subject: Cloud Computing
title: In-Memory Caching with Redis
description: One-minute skill: In-Memory Caching with Redis.

hook.text: A database query takes 50 milliseconds. The same data from Redis takes 0.5 milliseconds. That's 100x faster.

buildup.text: Redis stores data in RAM instead of on disk. Memory is thousands of times faster than solid-state drives.

discovery.text: Redis handles session data, leaderboards, rate limiting, and real-time analytics — anything that needs speed.

twist.text: RAM is expensive and limited. You can't cache everything. Choosing what to cache — and when to evict — is the art.

climax.text: ElastiCache, MemoryDB, and Azure Cache for Redis make it managed. You get the speed without the operational overhead.

punchline.text: Redis is fast because RAM is fast. Cache wisely.

quiz.question: Why is Redis so much faster than traditional databases?
options: It stores data in RAM, which is thousands of times faster than disk
It uses a special compression algorithm that speeds up queries
It only supports simple data types that are faster to process

details.summary: Redis is an in-memory data store used as a cache, session store, and message broker. Cloud-managed versions like ElastiCache and MemoryDB provide microsecond latency without managing Redis clusters yourself. Caching can reduce database load by over 90 percent.
details.whyItMatters: In-memory caching is the single most effective way to improve application performance. Redis has become the default caching layer for cloud applications worldwide.
takeaways: Stores data in memory for microsecond response times
Reduces database load by serving repeated queries from cache
Managed services handle clustering, failover, and patching

faq.question: What is the difference between Redis and Memcached?
faq.answer: Redis supports complex data structures like sorted sets, lists, and hashes, plus persistence and replication. Memcached is simpler, supporting only key-value strings with multi-threaded performance. Redis is more versatile; Memcached can be faster for simple caching.

faq.question: How do you handle cache invalidation with Redis?
faq.answer: Set TTLs on cached entries so stale data expires automatically. Use pub/sub or event-driven invalidation to remove entries when the source data changes. Cache-aside pattern gives the application explicit control over when to populate and invalidate cache entries.
